title: Китайская экскурсия и обещание Макса  (The Chinese Tour Group and Max's Promise)

segments.t: Vika rushes into the kitchen in a panic to tell Max that an entire busload of Chinese tourists has just sat down expecting lunch while the Chef is gone and Lyova is on vacation. As Vika grabs her phone to call Nagiyev, Max begs her to trust him to save the service.
Шеф уехал, су-шеф в отпуске, а остальные...
Let's replay the exchange and look closely at each Russian phrase.
'We have guests in the dining room.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'by' before landing on 'guests'.
'There was supposed to be one and a half people today.' In Russian, the idea of 'one and a half' flows naturally into 'maybe' without extra filler words. Dmitry answers right away.
'A whole tour group just arrived.' Dmitry anchors the line on 'by', while 'have come' completes the thought.
'Do you understand what kind of situation this is?' Chef Viktor anchors the line on 'do you understand', while 'matter' completes the thought.
Шеф уехал, су-шеф в отпуске, а остальные...
'The Chef left, the sous-chef is on vacation, and the rest...' The '-l' ending on the verb meaning 'left' places the action in the masculine past tense. Dmitry answers right away.
'Wait, why is that?' The grammar packs 'and' and 'why' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange.
'Have you all lost your minds?' Chef Viktor anchors the line on 'you', while 'went' completes the thought.
'The acting sous-chef is right here on duty.' Notice how Russian expresses 'any minute' and 'place' with crisp inflection rather than helper words. Dmitry answers right away.
'Alright, that is it.' Dmitry anchors the line on 'like this', while 'all' completes the thought.
'I am calling Dmitriy Vladimirovich right now.' In Russian, the idea of 'call' flows naturally into 'Vladimirovich' without extra filler words.
'Vika, please do not.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'Vika' before landing on 'at'. Dmitry answers right away.
'Vika, I will solve this problem myself.' The grammar packs 'Vika' and 'problem' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange.
'Trust me, please.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'believe' and finishing on 'there you go'. Let's hear the complete conversation once more.
Шеф уехал, су-шеф в отпуске, а остальные...
